stem: A company has just paid an annual dividend of USD 1.50. Dividends are expected to grow at 5% a year indefinitely, and the required return on equity is 9%. The intrinsic value per share using the Gordon growth model is closest to:

rationale.A: Incorrect. This uses D0 = 1.50 instead of next year's dividend D1 in the numerator.
rationale.B: Correct. Next year's dividend of 1.575 divided by r − g of 4% gives 39.38.
rationale.C: Incorrect. This divides D1 by r − g computed as 6% (for example 0.09 − 0.03), misreading the growth rate.

stem: A stock has just paid a dividend of USD 1.00. Dividends will grow at 20% a year for the next two years and at 5% a year thereafter. The required return is 11%. The intrinsic value per share is closest to:

rationale.A: Incorrect. This computes the terminal value as D2/(r − g) instead of D3/(r − g), forgetting to grow the dividend one more year.
rationale.B: Incorrect. This adds the terminal value of 25.20 without discounting it back two years.
rationale.C: Correct. Discounting D1, D2 and the year-2 terminal value of 25.20 at 11% gives 22.70.

stem: A company earns a return on equity of 15% and pays out 40% of its earnings as dividends. Its sustainable growth rate is closest to:

rationale.A: Correct. The firm retains 60% of earnings and reinvests them at 15%, so g = 9.00%.
rationale.B: Incorrect. This multiplies ROE by the payout ratio instead of the retention ratio.
rationale.C: Incorrect. This equals ROE, which would only be the growth rate if the firm retained all earnings.

stem: An analyst is valuing a profitable, fast-growing technology company that has never paid a dividend and does not plan to for several years. Which present value approach is most appropriate?
options: A Gordon growth model applied to the current dividend
A free cash flow to equity model
explanation: When a firm pays no dividends, or dividends do not reflect its earning power, discounting free cash flow to equity captures the cash available to shareholders.

rationale.A: Incorrect. With no current dividend and growth well above any sustainable rate, a single-stage dividend model is unusable.
rationale.B: Incorrect. A perpetuity model suits a fixed-dividend preferred share, not a growing common share with no dividend.
rationale.C: Correct. FCFE measures cash available to equity holders regardless of the firm's dividend policy.
